title: Oracle-bone eclipse and star records
creator: Shang royal diviners
location: Anyang, Henan; fragments in many collections
description: Among the tens of thousands of inscribed bones and shells excavated since 1899 at the late Shang capital of Yin, near Anyang, a few dozen refer to eclipses of the moon and sun, to stars and to unusual weather, usually as omens on which the king sought advice. They are dated by the ganzhi cycle of sixty days that the Shang used continuously, and are the earliest evidence for that count. One famous inscription mentions a 'great new star' beside the asterism Huo, sometimes read as a nova. Because the dates can be correlated with eclipse calculations, the records have been used both to fix Shang chronology and to measure the slowing of the earth's rotation, though the readings of particular characters remain debated.

title: Huangdi Neijing
creator: Authors of the Huangdi Neijing
location: China; Suwen edited by Wang Bing, 762
description: The Huangdi Neijing survives in two parts, the Suwen ('Basic Questions') and the Lingshu ('Spiritual Pivot'), each of 81 chapters, mostly cast as dialogues between the Yellow Emperor and his physicians Qibo and others. Compiled from many shorter texts, probably between the third and first centuries BC, it presents the body as a microcosm governed by yin and yang and the five phases, with organs linked to seasons, colours, tastes and emotions, and with qi and blood circulating through twelve main channels. Disease arises from imbalance caused by climate, emotion or diet; the physician diagnoses by observation and the pulse and treats with needles, moxibustion and drugs, ideally before illness appears. Edited and expanded by Wang Bing in the Tang and by the Song editorial office, it remains the theoretical root of Chinese, Korean and Japanese traditional medicine.

title: Zhoubi Suanjing
creator: Authors of the Zhoubi Suanjing
description: The Zhoubi Suanjing, 'Mathematical Classic of the Zhou Gnomon', is a short text compiled under the Western Han from older material. It sets out the gaitian or 'canopy heaven' cosmology, in which the heavens are a dome rotating over a flat earth, and computes the distance of the sun from the length of the noon shadow of an eight-foot gnomon at different places, assuming that the shadow changes by one inch for every thousand li. Its first section, a dialogue between the Duke of Zhou and Shang Gao, contains the gougu rule for right triangles and the famous 'hypotenuse diagram' that demonstrates it for the 3-4-5 triangle. With commentaries by Zhao Shuang and later Li Chunfeng, it became one of the Ten Computational Canons of the Tang examinations.

title: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art
creator: Authors of the Nine Chapters
description: Jiuzhang Suanshu is a collection of 246 practical problems, each with an answer and a general procedure, arranged in nine chapters: field measurement, millet and rice exchange, distribution by proportion, short width, construction works, fair levies, excess and deficit, rectangular arrays and right triangles. Its methods include adding fractions, finding square and cube roots, computing volumes of solids, the rule of false position and, in the chapter fangcheng, solving systems of linear equations by elimination on a rectangular array of counting rods, with rules for positive and negative numbers. The text gives no proofs; Liu Hui's commentary of 263 supplied justifications. It shaped mathematical teaching in China for over a millennium and was studied in Korea and Japan; the Tang made it the chief text of the mathematics examination.

title: Shennong Bencao Jing
creator: Authors of the Shennong Bencao Jing
description: The Shennong Bencao Jing is the oldest work in the bencao tradition of Chinese pharmacology. It lists 365 drugs, one for each day of the year, of which some 250 are plants, the rest animals and minerals, and divides them into superior, middle and inferior classes according to whether they nourish life, strengthen the body or attack disease. For each it gives the taste, the 'temperature' and the conditions it treats, and it states rules for combining drugs. The original text is lost; around 500 Tao Hongjing edited it with additions, and later pharmacopoeias absorbed it, so modern versions are reconstructions. Its scheme of grading drugs by toxicity and effect shaped all later Chinese materia medica.

title: Invention of paper
creator: Cai Lun
description: Paper is made by beating plant fibres in water until they separate, catching the pulp on a fine screen and drying the mat into a sheet. Fragments of hemp paper from western China date from the second century BC, used at first for wrapping, but the Han history credits the court eunuch Cai Lun with presenting in 105 a paper made from mulberry bark, hemp waste, rags and old fishing nets, and he is remembered as its inventor. Over the next centuries paper replaced bamboo strips and silk for writing in China. Papermaking reached Korea and Japan by about the seventh century, Samarkand and Baghdad in the eighth, and Spain and Italy in the twelfth and thirteenth, where it made the printing revolution possible.

title: Water-powered armillary sphere
creator: Zhang Heng
description: Zhang Heng, as Grand Astrologer, built an armillary or celestial globe whose rings represented the equator, the ecliptic and the horizon, and connected it to an inflow water clock so that it rotated in time with the heavens; observers inside could call out to those on the platform outside when a star rose or set. His writings on it survive only in fragments. The device began a long Chinese tradition of water-driven astronomical machines that led through Yi Xing to Su Song's clock tower.

title: Seismoscope
creator: Zhang Heng
description: According to the History of the Later Han, in 132 Zhang Heng presented to the court a bronze vessel like a wine jar, about two metres across, with eight dragons around its body facing the directions of the compass, each holding a ball above an open-mouthed toad. When an earthquake occurred, a mechanism inside, probably a pendulum, released one ball, indicating the direction of the shock. The history tells that once a ball fell when no tremor was felt in Luoyang, and days later a messenger reported an earthquake in Longxi to the west. The instrument is lost and its interior is not described, so modern reconstructions differ; it is nonetheless recognised as the first known seismoscope.

title: Shanghan Zabing Lun
creator: Zhang Zhongjing
location: China; later divided into Shanghan Lun and Jingui Yaolüe
description: Written around 200–210 amid the epidemics of the late Han, Zhang Zhongjing's treatise was scattered in the following wars and rearranged by Wang Shuhe; the Song editorial office printed it in two parts, the Treatise on Cold Damage (Shanghan Lun) and the Essentials from the Golden Cabinet (Jingui Yaolüe). The first describes the progression of feverish illness through six stages, from the 'greater yang' on the surface to the 'reverting yin' deep in the body, each defined by a set of signs, and gives 113 prescriptions with exact ingredients and preparation. The method of 'pattern identification and treatment' it embodies remains the core of Chinese clinical medicine, and from the seventeenth century its formulas became the basis of the Japanese koihō school of kampō.

title: South-pointing chariot
creator: Ma Jun
description: The south-pointing chariot carried a figure with an outstretched arm that pointed in one direction however the vehicle turned. Legends credited it to the Yellow Emperor, but the first reliable accounts concern Ma Jun, who built one for the Wei court around 235 after a debate about whether such a thing was possible. Since it used no magnet, it must have worked by gears linking the two wheels, so that when one wheel moved further than the other in a turn, the figure turned by the same angle the other way; this amounts to a differential gear. Later versions were built under the Song, when the engineers Yan Su and Wu Deren left detailed descriptions of the gearing.

title: Liu Hui's commentary and π by polygons
creator: Liu Hui
description: In 263 Liu Hui completed a commentary on the Nine Chapters that explained the reasoning behind each procedure, using cut-and-rearrange dissections of plane and solid figures, which he described as pieces of coloured paper or blocks. For the area of the circle he inscribed a hexagon and repeatedly doubled its sides, arguing that 'cut after cut', the polygon finally coincides with the circle, and obtained 3.14 and then 3.1416. His treatment of the volume of a pyramid used a limiting process, and his appendix on surveying became the separate Sea Island Mathematical Manual. The commentary was printed with the Nine Chapters and is the earliest surviving Chinese mathematical writing to argue for its results.

title: Pulse Classic (Maijing)
creator: Wang Shuhe
description: Wang Shuhe's Maijing, in ten chapters, gathered earlier teaching on the pulse into a method: the physician feels the radial pulse at three positions on each wrist, at three depths, each related to particular organs, and distinguishes twenty-four types such as floating, sinking, slippery and choppy. The book links these types to diseases and prognoses, drawing on the Inner Classic, the Classic of Difficulties and Zhang Zhongjing. It became a required text of the Tang medical bureau, was carried to Korea and Japan, and passed in translation through Persia, where a version appears in the fourteenth-century compilation of Rashid al-Din.

title: Baopuzi
creator: Ge Hong
description: The inner chapters of the Baopuzi, finished around 317, argue that immortality can be attained and describe how: by breathing exercises, diet, sexual practice, talismans and above all by elixirs made from cinnabar, gold, mercury and other minerals refined in sealed crucibles over long periods. Ge Hong quotes recipes from older alchemical scriptures and describes experiments such as the transformation of cinnabar into mercury and back. The outer chapters discuss politics and morality in Confucian terms. With his medical handbook, it is the main source for early Chinese alchemy and its practical chemistry.

title: Zu Chongzhi's calculation of π
creator: Zu Chongzhi
description: The Sui dynastic history records that Zu Chongzhi showed that π lies between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, and gave 22/7 as an 'approximate ratio' and 355/113 as a 'close ratio'. His book Zhui Shu, which explained his methods, was lost by the Song, but he probably extended Liu Hui's method of inscribed polygons to one of 12,288 or 24,576 sides, a huge labour on the counting board. The fraction 355/113 was not found again in Europe until the sixteenth century, and his decimal bounds were not bettered until Jamshid al-Kashi in 1424. In China the fraction is known as the Zu ratio.

title: Qimin Yaoshu
creator: Jia Sixie
description: Jia Sixie's book, in ten chapters and ninety-two sections, describes the cultivation of grains, legumes, vegetables and fruit, tree grafting, the raising of silkworms, horses, cattle, sheep and fish, and the making of vinegar, wine, soy sauce, pickles and other foods, mostly for the dry north of China. It records crop rotation, green manuring and the selection of seed, quotes about 160 earlier works, many otherwise lost, and adds the author's own observations. It is a key source for Chinese agricultural and culinary history and the model for later official farming manuals.

title: Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold
creator: Sun Simiao
description: Sun Simiao named his book on the principle that a human life is worth more than a thousand pieces of gold. In thirty chapters it treats gynaecology and obstetrics first, then paediatrics, then internal medicine, acupuncture, diet and longevity, with over 5,000 prescriptions; a supplement of 682 adds more than 2,000 others. It describes goitre treated with seaweed and thyroid tissue and night blindness treated with liver, and opens with 'On the Absolute Sincerity of Great Physicians', a statement of medical ethics still quoted in Chinese medical schools. Both works were central texts of later Chinese and Japanese medicine.

title: Dunhuang Star Chart
creator: Tang astronomers of the Dunhuang star chart
location: Dunhuang, Tang China; now British Library, London
description: The Dunhuang star chart is a paper scroll found in the Mogao 'Library Cave', sealed around 1000, and now in the British Library. After a section of cloud divinations it maps the whole sky visible from China in thirteen panels: twelve strips along the equator, one for each Jupiter station, drawn in a projection similar to the cylindrical, and a circular map of the polar region. About 1,300 stars are shown in 257 asterisms, coloured red, black and yellow according to the three ancient star catalogues of Shi Shen, Gan De and Wu Xian. Dating by the script and taboo characters points to the late seventh century. Its accuracy shows that it was copied from careful astronomical originals.

title: Dayan calendar and meridian survey
creator: Yi Xing
description: Between 723 and 726 Yi Xing and the astronomer Nangong Yue organised teams who measured the summer-solstice noon shadow of a standard gnomon and the altitude of the pole star at stations from Jiaozhou in modern Vietnam to the Mongolian steppe. The results showed that the old rule of one inch of shadow per thousand li was false, and gave a value for a degree of meridian arc of about 130 km, too long but a remarkable first measurement. With the data and new observations Yi Xing compiled the Dayan calendar, finished at his death in 727 and issued in 729, which was praised as the model of Tang calendrical science and adopted in Japan.

title: Gunpowder
creator: Daoist alchemists
description: Gunpowder seems to have been discovered by alchemists heating saltpetre with sulphur and carbonaceous materials in search of elixirs; a ninth-century text warns of the fires such mixtures cause. By the tenth century it was used in incendiary arrows, and the Wujing Zongyao of 1044 gives the first recipes. Over the following centuries the Song, Jin and Mongols developed fire lances, exploding bombs, rockets and, by the late thirteenth century, metal-barrelled guns; the oldest surviving bronze guns date from about 1290. The Mongol conquests and trade carried knowledge of gunpowder west, and it appears in European and Islamic sources in the second half of the thirteenth century, with transformative effects on warfare everywhere.

title: Ishinpō
creator: Tanba no Yasuyori
location: Heian-kyō (Kyoto), Japan; Nakarai family manuscript in the Tokyo National Museum
description: Tanba no Yasuyori compiled the Ishinpō, 'Essential Methods of Medicine', from extracts of more than a hundred Chinese medical texts of the Six Dynasties, Sui and Tang, arranged by subject: general principles, acupuncture, diseases of each part of the body, women's and children's medicine, pharmacy, diet, longevity and the bedchamber. Each passage is cited by source, and since many of these works were later lost in China, the Ishinpō is a primary witness to early Chinese medicine. The finest manuscript, handed down in the Nakarai family of physicians, was bought by the Japanese state in 1982 and designated a National Treasure.

title: Movable type
creator: Bi Sheng
description: Woodblock printing, used in China since the seventh or eighth century, required carving a whole block for every page. Bi Sheng instead made a separate piece for each character in clay, hardening them by fire. He placed the types side by side in an iron frame on an iron plate coated with pine resin, wax and paper ash, warmed it to soften the coating, pressed the type flat with a board and printed; while one frame printed, another was set. Common characters had twenty or more copies. Shen Kuo, who describes it, says that for a few copies it was not fast, but for hundreds or thousands it was very quick. No books printed with his type survive, and in China wooden type, used by Wang Zhen, and later bronze type remained a secondary method; in Korea movable metal type became central.

title: Wujing Zongyao
creator: Zeng Gongliang
description: Commissioned by Emperor Renzong after a defeat by the Western Xia, the Wujing Zongyao was compiled by Zeng Gongliang, Ding Du and others and completed in 1044. Its forty chapters cover strategy, organisation, fortification, naval warfare, signalling and weapons, with many illustrations of crossbows, siege engines, ships and flamethrowers. Three recipes describe gunpowder for an incendiary ball, a poison-smoke ball and a thorn-studded bomb, with saltpetre making up roughly half the mixture. The book also explains how to make a thin iron leaf in the shape of a fish magnetic by heating and quenching it in the earth's field, and float it on water to find south. The surviving editions are Ming reprints, and some illustrations may have been redrawn.

title: Dream Pool Essays
creator: Shen Kuo
description: Shen Kuo wrote the Mengxi Bitan in retirement at his estate, the Dream Brook, and it was published around 1088, with two supplements. Its entries mix anecdote and history with first-hand observation. He describes the magnetic needle, suspended by a silk thread, and notes that it points slightly east of south; explains the formation of mountains and alluvial plains by erosion and sedimentation, citing marine fossils high inland; infers climate change from petrified bamboo in the dry north; discusses the camera obscura and concave mirrors; works out the sum of stacked objects and the length of arcs; and records Bi Sheng's movable type and the iron-smelting and oil of his time. Its range has made it a favourite source for historians of Chinese science.

title: Su Song's astronomical clock tower
creator: Su Song
description: Su Song's tower stood in the Song capital Kaifeng from about 1090. On its open roof was a bronze armillary sphere for observation; in the middle storey a celestial globe turned in step with the sky; below, a five-tiered pagoda displayed jacks that rang bells, struck gongs and held up tablets to mark the hours and quarters. All were driven by a large waterwheel with 36 scoops, filled one at a time from a constant-level tank and released by a weighbridge and trip lever acting as an escapement, so that the wheel advanced in regular steps. A chain drive transmitted the power upward. The tower was dismantled after the Jurchen captured Kaifeng in 1127, and no later Chinese builder matched it, but Su Song's book made full-scale reconstructions possible in the twentieth century.

title: Xin Yixiang Fayao
creator: Su Song
description: Su Song wrote the Xin Yixiang Fayao to record the design of his clock tower so that it could be built again. In three chapters it gives an overview drawing of the tower and some fifty detailed drawings of the armillary, the globe, the waterwheel, the escapement, the chain drive and the jacks, with dimensions. It also includes five star maps showing over 1,400 stars, among the oldest printed star charts. The book survived in later copies, and its drawings allowed Joseph Needham and others to explain the mechanism and to build working models.

title: Magnetic compass
creator: Chinese compass makers
description: Chinese texts describe the attraction of lodestone by the third century BC, and Han and later diviners may have used a lodestone spoon on a board for geomancy, though the evidence is disputed. By the eleventh century both the floating iron fish of the Wujing Zongyao and Shen Kuo's needle rubbed on lodestone were known, and Shen Kuo observed magnetic declination, the difference between magnetic and true south. Zhu Yu's Pingzhou Ketan, written about 1117 about Guangzhou around 1100, records that pilots used the needle at night or in overcast weather. The compass appears in European writing by Alexander Neckam about 1190 and in the Islamic world soon after. It made open-sea navigation possible and, with gunpowder and printing, figures in Francis Bacon's list of inventions that changed the world.

title: Collected Cases of Injustice Rectified
creator: Song Ci
description: Drawing on earlier case collections and his own experience as a judicial commissioner, Song Ci wrote the Xi Yuan Ji Lu in 1247 to guide officials who had to examine deaths. It explains how to conduct an inquest, how to distinguish suicide, murder and accident, how to recognise wounds made before and after death, signs of drowning, burning, hanging and strangulation, and the effects of poisons, and how to reveal bruises with vinegar and heated pits. Some of its methods, such as testing for bloodstains, have been tested by modern scientists, others are unreliable. Expanded by later editions, it remained the official coroners' manual of China until the twentieth century and was translated into Korean, Japanese, Dutch, French, German and English.

title: Mathematical Treatise in Nine Sections
creator: Qin Jiushao
description: Qin Jiushao's Shushu Jiuzhang contains 81 problems in nine sections on calendars, land, surveying, taxes, construction, military matters and trade, many deliberately complicated. The first section gives the dayan qiuyi method for finding a number with given remainders when divided by several numbers, including non-coprime ones, a full solution of what became known as the Chinese remainder theorem, used for calendar computations. Other problems lead to polynomial equations up to the tenth degree, solved on the counting board by a step-by-step procedure equivalent to Horner's method of 1819. The book also gives Qin's formula for the area of a triangle from its sides, equivalent to Heron's. It circulated in manuscript and was printed only in 1842.

title: Sea Mirror of Circle Measurements
creator: Li Ye
description: The Ceyuan Haijing begins with a single diagram, a right triangle with a circle inscribed and many smaller triangles, and then poses 170 problems about the diameter of a circular city from distances walked by people leaving its gates. Li Ye sets up each problem by the tianyuan shu, the 'method of the celestial element', in which the coefficients of an equation in one unknown are written in a vertical column of counting-rod numerals, with negatives marked by a slanted stroke and zero by a circle. He solves equations up to the sixth degree. The book and his later Yigu Yanduan are the principal sources for northern Chinese algebra of the thirteenth century.

title: Yang Hui's triangle
creator: Yang Hui
description: In his Xiangjie Jiuzhang Suanfa of 1261, Yang Hui reproduced a diagram he attributed to the eleventh-century mathematician Jia Xian, showing the coefficients for expanding (a + b) to the sixth power in a triangle in which each number is the sum of the two above it. Jia Xian used it to extract roots of high order. The same triangle had appeared in India and the Islamic world, notably in the work of al-Karaji and al-Samaw'al, and was later treated by Blaise Pascal in 1654. In China it is called the Yang Hui or Jia Xian triangle, and Zhu Shijie printed it to the eighth power in 1303.

title: Shoushi calendar
creator: Guo Shoujing
description: After the Mongol conquest Khubilai Khan ordered a new calendar, and a commission led by Wang Xun and Guo Shoujing worked from 1276 to 1280. Guo designed new bronze instruments, including the simplified armillary and an enlarged gnomon with a pinhole shadow-definer that measured the solstice shadow precisely, and observations were taken at twenty-seven stations across the empire. The resulting Shoushi calendar, promulgated in 1281, adopted a tropical year of 365.2425 days and used third-order interpolation for the motions of the sun and moon and a form of spherical trigonometry. Renamed the Datong calendar under the Ming, it was used until 1644, and Korea's Chiljeongsan was adapted from it.

title: Songjiang cotton technology
creator: Huang Daopo
description: Cotton reached China from South and Southeast Asia and was grown in the south long before it became common in the Yangzi valley in the thirteenth century. According to the Yuan writer Tao Zongyi, the women of Songjiang had only crude methods until Huang Daopo returned from Hainan and taught them how to remove seeds with a roller gin, loosen the fibre with a bow, spin with a treadle wheel carrying three spindles, and weave patterned cloth. Within a century Songjiang cloth was famous throughout China, and cotton replaced hemp as the main clothing fibre of ordinary people. How much is owed to one woman is uncertain, but her story records a real transfer of technique from the Li people of Hainan.

title: Jade Mirror of the Four Unknowns
creator: Zhu Shijie
description: The Siyuan Yujian presents 288 problems solved by the 'method of four elements', in which up to four unknowns, named heaven, earth, man and matter, are arranged around a central constant term on the counting board, so that each square holds the coefficient of a product of powers. Zhu Shijie eliminates unknowns step by step to reach a single equation in one unknown, which he solves numerically, and he also sums finite series, such as piles of stacked balls, using what are now called finite differences. The book opens with the arithmetical triangle, labelled the 'ancient method'. Little understood under the Ming, it was recovered in the nineteenth century and studied by both Chinese and Western historians of mathematics.

title: Nong Shu and wooden movable type
creator: Wang Zhen
description: Wang Zhen's Nong Shu, completed in 1313, combines a general treatise on farming in north and south China, an account of individual crops, and a long illustrated section on implements: ploughs, harrows, seed drills, irrigation wheels, water-powered trip-hammers, mills and bellows, and machines for silk and hemp. It is one of the main sources for Chinese engineering before modern times. Appended to it is his essay on printing with wooden movable type, describing how he had more than 60,000 characters carved, sorted them on two large revolving tables by rhyme, and printed a gazetteer of Jingde county in 1298 in less than a month. It is the earliest detailed description of a working movable-type printing shop.

title: Cheonsang Yeolcha Bunyajido
creator: Joseon royal astronomers
location: Hanseong (Seoul), Joseon; now National Palace Museum of Korea
description: According to its inscription by Gwon Geun, the chart was carved for King Taejo, founder of Joseon, from a rubbing of an old Goguryeo star map whose stone had been lost in a river, corrected with new observations by the royal astronomers. The stele, about two metres tall, shows a circular map of the sky centred on the north pole, with the 28 lunar lodges, the equator and the ecliptic, and some 1,467 stars, followed by texts on the lodges, the twelve stations and the stars culminating at dusk and dawn in each season. It legitimised the new dynasty by showing its alignment with heaven. A second carving was made under King Sukjong in 1687. Both stones survive in Seoul, and rubbings and printed copies spread widely; it appears on the 10,000-won note.

title: Nongsa Jikseol
creator: Sejong the Great
description: Sejong found that Chinese farming manuals did not suit Korean soils and climate, and in 1428 ordered provincial governors to ask old farmers about their practices. The official Jeong Cho edited the results into the Nongsa Jikseol, printed in 1429 and distributed to local officials. It describes the preparation of seed, ploughing, manuring, and the cultivation of rice, millet, beans, barley and other crops, including transplanting and dry sowing of rice. It is the first Korean agricultural book written from Korean experience.

title: Hyangyak Jipseongbang
creator: Sejong the Great
description: Imported Chinese drugs were expensive and scarce, and Korean physicians had long sought local substitutes, hyangyak. In 1431–33 the scholars Yu Hyo-tong, No Jung-rye and Pak Yun-deok compiled the Hyangyak Jipseongbang in 85 chapters, listing 959 disease patterns and over 10,000 prescriptions drawn from Korean and Chinese books, with 694 local drugs. Officials were sent with the embassy to China to check the identity of Korean plants. With the later Uibang Yuchwi, a huge medical encyclopedia of 1445, it laid the basis for Heo Jun's Dongui Bogam.

title: Jagyeongnu
creator: Jang Yeong-sil
description: Built by Jang Yeong-sil and Kim Bin at Sejong's command and installed in 1434 in the Borugak pavilion of Gyeongbok Palace, the Jagyeongnu was the official timekeeper of Joseon. Water flowed from large vessels into two cylinders in which floats rose, pushing rods that released copper balls at set intervals. The balls rolled down channels to trip a mechanism of levers and further balls that made three wooden figures strike a bell for the double-hours and a drum and gong for the night watches, while figures holding time-tablets appeared. The design drew on Chinese and Islamic water clocks. The original was destroyed, and a version made in 1536 survives in part at Deoksu Palace; full working reconstructions have been built in Seoul.

title: Angbu Ilgu
creator: Jang Yeong-sil
description: The Angbu Ilgu is a hemispherical bronze sundial with a pointed gnomon aimed at the celestial pole; the shadow of its tip falls on a grid of seven vertical hour lines and thirteen curving lines for the solar terms of the year. Sejong placed such sundials in public streets of Seoul in 1434, with the hours marked by animal figures of the zodiac so that people who could not read could tell the time. They were made by Jang Yeong-sil and other court craftsmen, building on Yuan models. Several later examples from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries survive, and it is one of the symbols of Joseon science.

title: Cheugugi rain gauge
creator: Sejong the Great
description: In 1441 Sejong's government, at the suggestion of Crown Prince Munjong, made a cylinder of iron or bronze of fixed size, about 30 cm tall and 14 cm across, and the next year installed it on a stone base at the royal observatory and at every provincial and county office. After each rain, officials measured the depth of water with a ruler and reported it to the capital, and the records were used to plan farming and assess taxes. The system, revived in the eighteenth century, produced a continuous Korean rainfall record from 1777. The only surviving cheugugi, made in 1837 for Gongju, is a national treasure of Korea. It predates Benedetto Castelli's rain gauge of 1639.

title: Chiljeongsan
creator: Sejong the Great
description: Sejong ordered his astronomers Yi Sun-ji and Kim Dam and others to master the Chinese Shoushi system and the Islamic Huihui calendar and adapt them to Korea. The result, the Chiljeongsan Naepyeon and Oepyeon, was completed in 1442. It calculated the positions of the sun, moon and five visible planets, eclipses and the times of sunrise and sunset for Seoul, so that Korea no longer depended on Chinese predictions. It shows the high mathematical level of the Sejong court and was used until the Shixian calendar was adopted in 1653.

title: Bencao Gangmu
creator: Li Shizhen
description: Li Shizhen worked on the Bencao Gangmu for nearly three decades, finishing it in 1578; it was printed in Nanjing in 1596, three years after his death. In 52 chapters it describes 1,892 drugs, 374 of them newly added, arranged in sixteen divisions from water, fire and earth through minerals, herbs, grains, vegetables, fruit and trees to insects, fish, birds, beasts and humans, with an entry for each giving names, origin, preparation, properties and uses. Li corrected many errors of earlier pharmacopoeias, rejected some claims of immortality drugs and gave careful descriptions of plants and animals, making it the greatest work of Chinese natural history as well as pharmacology. Reprinted many times, it shaped honzōgaku, the study of natural products, in Edo Japan, and was partly translated into Latin, French, English and Russian.

title: Exact equal temperament
creator: Zhu Zaiyu
description: For two thousand years Chinese music theory generated its twelve pitches by cycles of fifths, which never return exactly to the starting note. In his Lülü Jingyi of 1584 and later Yuelü Quanshu, the Ming prince Zhu Zaiyu showed that dividing the octave into twelve equal semitones requires each pipe or string to be shorter than the last by the twelfth root of two, and calculated the lengths to twenty-five digits by extracting square and cube roots on a large abacus. He also built a set of tuned pipes and corrected lengths for the end effect of pipes. Simon Stevin reached the same idea in Europe at about the same time; whether either knew of the other is debated.

title: Kunyu Wanguo Quantu
creator: Matteo Ricci
description: Ricci made a first world map in Chinese at Zhaoqing in 1584, and in 1602 in Beijing, with the official Li Zhizao, printed a large version on six panels about 3.6 metres wide. Based on European maps such as those of Ortelius, it placed China near the centre by putting the Pacific in the middle, showed the five continents, gave notes on many countries and explained the spherical earth, latitude and longitude, and the size of the globe. Copies were made in colour for the Wanli Emperor, and versions reached Korea and Japan, where they shaped geographical knowledge for two centuries. Only a few original prints survive, including one in the James Ford Bell Library in Minnesota.

title: Jihe Yuanben (Euclid's Elements)
creator: Matteo Ricci
description: Working from his teacher Clavius's Latin edition of Euclid, Ricci explained the text orally and Xu Guangqi wrote it in classical Chinese, in sessions over about a year; the first six books, on plane geometry, were printed in Beijing in 1607 as Jihe Yuanben, 'Origins of Quantity'. They had to invent much of the vocabulary, including the word jihe, now the Chinese and Japanese word for geometry, and terms for point, line, angle and parallel. Xu praised the work for its rigour, saying it could not be doubted, refuted or improved; Chinese mathematics had not used axiomatic proof of this kind. The remaining nine books were translated only in 1857 by Li Shanlan and Alexander Wylie.

title: Dongui Bogam
creator: Heo Jun
description: Commissioned by King Seonjo in 1596 and completed by Heo Jun in 1610, the Dongui Bogam was printed in 25 volumes in 1613. It is divided into five parts: internal bodily functions, external parts of the body, miscellaneous diseases, drugs and acupuncture. Heo Jun drew on over 200 Chinese and Korean medical books but organised them with an emphasis on nourishing life and preventing illness, and listed Korean names for 637 local drugs in the Korean alphabet so that ordinary people could find them. Reprinted many times in China and Japan, it remains the central text of Korean medicine, and it was added to the Memory of the World Register in 2009.

title: Jinkōki
creator: Yoshida Mitsuyoshi
description: Based on the Chinese Suanfa Tongzong (1592) of Cheng Dawei, the Jinkōki taught multiplication and division on the soroban, units of measure, the exchange of gold, silver and copper coins, interest, surveying, the calculation of rice and the volume of timber, with lively pictures and puzzles such as the multiplying of mice. It sold so well that it was pirated and revised for two centuries, and its name became a byword for an arithmetic book. In the 1641 edition Yoshida added twelve problems without answers, challenging readers; solving and posing such problems, idai keishō, became the engine of wasan.

title: Chongzhen calendar
creator: Xu Guangqi
description: After Xu Guangqi's prediction of a solar eclipse in 1629 proved more accurate than that of the official astronomers, the Chongzhen Emperor put him in charge of a new calendar bureau. With the Jesuits Johann Schreck, Giacomo Rho and Adam Schall, and Chinese scholars, he compiled the Chongzhen Lishu, 137 chapters on Tychonic planetary theory, spherical trigonometry, logarithm-free tables and instruments, presented between 1631 and 1634. The Ming fell before the calendar was adopted, but Schall presented a revised version to the Qing in 1645 as the Shixian calendar, and it guided Chinese astronomy for the next two centuries.

title: Tiangong Kaiwu
creator: Song Yingxing
description: In eighteen sections, arranged from things most needed for life to the least, Song Yingxing described the growing and processing of grain, clothing fibres and dyes, salt, sugar, oils, pottery, bronze casting, boats and carts, iron forging, lime and coal, paper, metal smelting, weapons including gunpowder, ink and pearls and jade. More than a hundred woodcuts show workers at furnaces, looms and mills. Song wrote from close observation and criticised scholars who scorned practical knowledge. Published in 1637, it was soon forgotten in Qing China but reprinted in Japan in 1771, where it influenced Edo technology; Chinese scholars recovered it from Japanese copies in the 1920s, and it is now a classic of the history of technology.

title: Nongzheng Quanshu
creator: Xu Guangqi
description: Xu Guangqi worked on agricultural questions for decades, experimenting with crops in Shanghai and Tianjin. His Nongzheng Quanshu, edited by Chen Zilong and published in 1639, has sixty chapters on land policy, soils, irrigation, tools, crops, sericulture, forestry, animal husbandry and famine plants. It includes the Taixi Shuifa, a treatise on Western hydraulic machines written with the Jesuit Sabatino de Ursis, and promotes the sweet potato, recently arrived from the Americas, as a famine crop. It became a standard work for officials concerned with food supply.

title: Shixian calendar
creator: Johann Adam Schall von Bell
description: When the Manchus entered Beijing in 1644, Schall offered the new rulers the calendar prepared under Xu Guangqi, and demonstrated its accuracy with an eclipse prediction. It was promulgated for 1645 as the Shixian li, 'Calendar of Temporal Models', with Schall as head of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau. Its foreign origin became the target of Yang Guangxian's attacks in 1664, but after Verbiest's tests the Kangxi Emperor restored it. With further revisions incorporating Kepler's ellipses in the eighteenth century, it was the basis of the official Chinese calendar until 1912, and it reached Korea, where it was adopted in 1653.

title: Instruments of the Beijing Ancient Observatory
creator: Ferdinand Verbiest
description: In 1669 the Kangxi Emperor ordered new instruments for the observatory on the city wall of Beijing, and Verbiest designed six on the pattern of those of Tycho Brahe: an ecliptic armillary sphere, an equatorial armillary sphere, an altazimuth, a quadrant, a sextant and a celestial globe, cast in bronze with dragons and clouds in Chinese style and installed in 1674. He described them in an illustrated work printed in Beijing. Later instruments were added in the eighteenth century. Several were taken to Germany and France after the Boxer War of 1900 and returned after the First World War; they can still be seen on the observatory platform.

title: Hatsubi Sanpō
creator: Seki Takakazu
description: In 1671 Sawaguchi Kazuyuki's Kokon Sanpōki ended with fifteen problems that seemed to require equations beyond the counting-board method of tengen jutsu, adopted from Zhu Shijie and Li Ye. Seki's Hatsubi Sanpō of 1674 solved all of them. Instead of rod numerals on a board, he wrote coefficients and unknowns on paper beside vertical lines, a notation later called bōsho-hō or endan-jutsu, which allowed equations with several unknowns and literal coefficients to be manipulated. Because it gave only the final equations without explanation, his pupil Takebe Katahiro published a commentary in 1685. It marks the beginning of a distinctively Japanese algebra.

title: Katsuyō Sanpō
creator: Seki Takakazu
description: Four years after Seki's death, his pupils Araki Murahide and Ōtaka Yoshimaro edited and printed his writings as Katsuyō Sanpō. It includes his work on sums of powers of integers, in which he gave a table of the coefficients now called Bernoulli numbers, printed a year before, and independently of, Jakob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi of 1713; work on regular polygons; and the calculation of π and arc length by series. His other manuscripts, circulated within the school, treat determinants, which he introduced in 1683, before Leibniz.

title: Lisuan Quanshu
creator: Mei Wending
type: Collected works on astronomy and mathematics
description: Mei Wending wrote some eighty works, many circulated in manuscript; after his death they were edited and printed in 1723 as Lisuan Quanshu, and later rearranged by his grandson Mei Juecheng as Meishi Congshu Jiyao. They explain Western plane and spherical trigonometry, geometry and planetary models clearly in Chinese terms, compare them with traditional methods, and recover forgotten Chinese techniques. Mei held that Western astronomy descended from ancient Chinese knowledge carried abroad, an idea that made it easier for scholars to accept. His books shaped the evidential scholars of the Qing and the mathematics studied in late Joseon Korea.

title: Uisan Mundap
creator: Hong Dae-yong
description: Written after Hong's journey to Beijing, the Uisan Mundap is a dialogue between a conventional scholar, Heo Ja, and a recluse, Silong, on Mount Yiwulü in Manchuria. Silong argues that the earth is a sphere that spins once a day, that there is no up and down in space, that the universe has no centre and holds countless worlds, and that since every country sees itself as the centre, the distinction between civilised China and barbarian others has no basis. Hong drew on Jesuit astronomy but went beyond it; the rotation of the earth was not taught by the Jesuits in China. It circulated in manuscript and became known widely only in the twentieth century.

title: Kaitai Shinsho
creator: Sugita Genpaku
description: After seeing a dissection in 1771 that matched the plates of a Dutch anatomy book rather than Chinese diagrams, Sugita Genpaku, Maeno Ryōtaku, Nakagawa Jun'an and others began translating the Ontleedkundige Tafelen, a Dutch version of the German anatomy of Johann Adam Kulmus. With only Maeno's limited Dutch and no dictionary, they worked for three and a half years, sometimes spending a day on one line. The result, published in four volumes of text and one of illustrations by Odano Naotake, introduced Japanese readers to European anatomy and coined words such as shinkei, nerve, still in use in Japanese and Chinese. Its success showed that Dutch books could be read and launched the movement of Dutch learning.

title: Erekiteru
creator: Hiraga Gennai
description: The elektriciteit, rendered in Japanese as erekiteru, was a box-shaped friction machine in which a crank turned a glass cylinder against a pad, generating static electricity that could be drawn off in sparks; Dutch traders had brought such devices as curiosities and for supposed medical use. Hiraga Gennai obtained a broken one in Nagasaki and after several years of work restored it in Edo in 1776, demonstrating sparks and shocks to paying visitors and patrons. He did not understand electrical theory, and the machine was mainly a spectacle, but it inspired later Japanese experimenters. One surviving erekiteru attributed to him is in the Postal Museum Japan.

title: Geojunggi crane
creator: Jeong Yak-yong
description: When King Jeongjo planned the fortress of Hwaseong at Suwon, he gave Jeong Yak-yong the Qing encyclopedia Gujin Tushu Jicheng, which reproduced a Jesuit book of Western machines. Jeong designed a crane, the geojunggi, using a set of upper and lower pulleys with two winches, with which a few men could lift heavy stones, and other devices for moving loads. The construction record, the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe of 1801, illustrates the crane and says the machines saved some 40,000 strings of cash. The fortress was finished in 1796 in under three years and is now a World Heritage Site.

title: General anaesthesia with tsūsensan
creator: Hanaoka Seishū
description: Hanaoka Seishū's tsūsensan, also called mafutsusan, was a decoction of six or more herbs, chiefly the datura plant chōsen-asagao and aconite, whose alkaloids produce deep unconsciousness. After years of animal tests and trials on his mother and wife, he gave it to Kan Aiya, a sixty-year-old woman with breast cancer, and excised the tumour while she was unconscious; she died some months later, probably of the disease. Hanaoka performed many more operations for breast cancer, as well as other surgery, and recorded them with illustrations. Because his school kept the formula secret and Japan was closed, the work was unknown in the West, where ether anaesthesia was demonstrated in 1846. It is now recognised by surgical and anaesthesiology societies worldwide.

title: Rangaku Kotohajime
creator: Sugita Genpaku
description: Written when Sugita was over eighty, Rangaku Kotohajime, 'The Beginnings of Dutch Learning', recounts the early contacts of Japanese physicians and interpreters with Dutch books, the dissection of 1771 at Kotsugahara, and the struggle to translate the anatomy text word by word, as well as the spread of rangaku afterwards. It circulated in manuscript until Fukuzawa Yukichi had it printed in 1869, presenting it as a story of Japan's early opening to Western science. It remains the classic account of the movement and a vivid picture of scholarly collaboration.

title: Maps of the coasts of Japan
creator: Inō Tadataka
location: Edo, Japan; Tokyo National Museum and other collections
description: Between 1800 and 1816 Inō and his teams walked some 35,000 km in ten expeditions, measuring distances with ropes, chains and counted paces, directions with magnetic compasses and latitudes by observing stars. The final maps, completed by his pupils in 1821 after his death, consisted of 214 sheets at about 1:36,000, 8 at 1:216,000 and 3 at 1:432,000, showing coastlines, roads, towns and landmarks with striking accuracy. Kept secret by the shogunate, they became famous when Siebold was caught with a copy in 1828; British surveyors in 1861 adopted them rather than complete their own. The government relied on them until the 1920s, and full sets of copies have been rediscovered in Japan and the United States.

title: Flora Japonica
creator: Philipp Franz von Siebold
description: From his years at Dejima, Siebold brought back to Europe thousands of herbarium specimens, seeds and living plants, as well as drawings by the Nagasaki artist Kawahara Keiga and others. With the Munich botanist Zuccarini he published Flora Japonica in instalments from 1835, with 150 hand-coloured plates describing hydrangeas, camellias, lilies, maples and many other species, several named for the first time. His companion works, Fauna Japonica and the multi-volume Nippon, described Japan's animals, geography and culture. His nursery in Leiden spread Japanese plants through Europe, and his collections are in Leiden and Munich.

title: Smallpox vaccination in Osaka
creator: Ogata Kōan
description: Cowpox vaccine first reached Japan successfully in 1849, when the Dutch physician Otto Mohnike in Nagasaki obtained viable lymph from Batavia. Within months Ogata Kōan and the merchant-physicians of Osaka opened the Jotōkan to vaccinate children free of charge, and Kōan sent vaccine to branch stations in many domains, overcoming fear and local resistance. In 1858 the shogunate recognised the centre officially, and the vaccination institute in Edo founded in the same year became the root of the University of Tokyo's medical faculty. The campaign was one of the first large public-health efforts in Japan.

title: Daedong Yeojido
creator: Kim Jeong-ho
description: The Daedong Yeojido was printed in 1861 from 60 woodblocks, some of which survive in the National Museum of Korea. It divides Korea from north to south into 22 strips, each folded like a screen into a book, which together form a map at a scale of about 1:160,000. Kim used a uniform grid, marked roads with dots at every ten li so that distances could be read, and used a legend of symbols for towns, fortresses, post stations, beacons and warehouses, while drawing mountains as continuous ridges. Built on earlier government and private maps and on his own gazetteer, it is the most accurate and practical traditional map of Korea.

title: Tetanus antitoxin and serum therapy
creator: Kitasato Shibasaburō
location: Robert Koch's Institute of Hygiene, Berlin
description: Working in Koch's laboratory, Kitasato in 1889 grew Clostridium tetani in pure culture by heating mixed cultures to kill other bacteria and growing the spores without oxygen, and showed that it produced a toxin. In December 1890 he and Emil von Behring published a paper showing that the blood serum of animals immunised with small doses of tetanus toxin protected other animals from the disease; Behring published similar work on diphtheria. Serum therapy became the first effective treatment for these infections and opened the field of immunology. Behring alone received the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1901, an omission that has often been discussed.

title: Identification of the plague bacillus
creator: Kitasato Shibasaburō
description: When plague broke out in Hong Kong in 1894, the Japanese government sent Kitasato with a team; he arrived on 12 June, a few days before the Swiss-French bacteriologist Yersin, and reported a bacillus in the blood of victims. Yersin, working separately, isolated the organism from buboes and described it more accurately, and the bacterium was later named Yersinia pestis. Kitasato's description contained confusions, possibly from contamination, and the priority has been debated; for some decades the organism was credited to both men. The episode marked Japan's arrival in international bacteriology.

title: Discovery of the dysentery bacillus
creator: Shiga Kiyoshi
description: In 1897 an epidemic of dysentery in Japan affected over 90,000 people and killed more than a fifth of them. Working at Kitasato's institute, Shiga Kiyoshi examined patients' stools and identified a bacillus that was agglutinated by the serum of patients but not of healthy people, showing that it was the cause. He published in Japanese in 1897 and in German in 1898. The genus Shigella was named after him, and the potent toxin produced by S. dysenteriae is called Shiga toxin. He went on to develop a vaccine and to work on chemotherapy with Paul Ehrlich.

title: Isolation of adrenaline
creator: Takamine Jōkichi
description: Extracts of the adrenal gland were known to raise blood pressure, and John Jacob Abel at Johns Hopkins had obtained an impure derivative he called epinephrine. In 1900 Takamine's assistant Uenaka Keizō succeeded in crystallising the active substance, and in 1901 Takamine patented and published it as adrenalin; it was the first hormone isolated in pure form. Marketed by Parke-Davis, it was soon used to stop bleeding in surgery and to treat asthma. Abel disputed the priority, and in the United States the name epinephrine was long preferred, while Uenaka's laboratory notebook later supported the Japanese claim.

title: Saturnian model of the atom
creator: Nagaoka Hantarō
description: In a lecture in Tokyo in 1903 and a paper in the Philosophical Magazine in 1904, Nagaoka rejected J. J. Thomson's model of electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge, proposing instead a large positive centre with electrons revolving in a ring around it, by analogy with Maxwell's analysis of the stability of Saturn's rings. He used the model to explain spectral lines and radioactivity. It faced the objection that orbiting electrons should radiate their energy and collapse, and he abandoned it, but in 1911 Ernest Rutherford cited Nagaoka when proposing the nuclear atom from scattering experiments.

title: Spirochaete in general paresis
creator: Noguchi Hideyo
location: Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, New York
description: General paresis, a progressive dementia with paralysis, filled asylums in the nineteenth century, and a link with past syphilis was suspected but unproven. In 1913 Noguchi and Joseph W. Moore published their finding of the syphilis spirochaete Treponema pallidum in the brain tissue of patients who had died of paresis, and Noguchi also found it in the spinal cord in tabes dorsalis. The discovery confirmed that these were late forms of syphilis and was one of the clearest demonstrations of an infectious cause of a mental illness. Several other claims by Noguchi were later shown to be wrong, but this one has stood.

title: Meson theory of nuclear forces
creator: Yukawa Hideki
location: Osaka Imperial University; Proceedings of the Physico-Mathematical Society of Japan
description: In his 1935 paper 'On the Interaction of Elementary Particles. I', Yukawa reasoned that just as the electromagnetic force is carried by photons, the strong force binding protons and neutrons should be carried by a field whose quanta have mass, since the force acts only over very short distances. From the range of nuclear forces he estimated the mass of the quantum at around 200 electron masses; the potential he introduced is still called the Yukawa potential. A particle of about that mass found in cosmic rays in 1937, the muon, turned out not to interact strongly, but the pion, discovered by Cecil Powell's group in 1947, fitted the prediction. Yukawa received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1949. The idea of force-carrying particles became central to modern particle physics.

title: Discovery of artemisinin
creator: Tu Youyou
location: Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Beijing
description: In Project 523 Tu Youyou's group screened some 2,000 traditional remedies for activity against malaria. Extracts of qinghao, Artemisia annua, gave inconsistent results until Tu, rereading Ge Hong's Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies, noticed that it called for steeping the plant in cold water, and reasoned that heat destroyed the active principle. In 1971 an ether extraction at low temperature completely cleared malaria parasites in mice and monkeys, Tu tested it on herself, and in 1972 the pure compound, qinghaosu or artemisinin, was isolated; its structure was determined later in the decade. Published mainly in Chinese during the Cultural Revolution, the work became widely known only later. Artemisinin-based combination therapies are now the standard treatment for malaria, and Tu shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2015.
